issues.failure_explanation: The proof of the equality case starts from equality and derives the block structure (blck) and the magnitudes and collinearity of the rows, so it proves only necessity. It never proves the converse: that a matrix with orthonormal columns whose rows are clustered as described has maximal sigma_2 exactly 1/sqrt(n). That needs, for rows in different groups, the inner product (u,v) from the zero-sum triangle relation p x+q y+r z=0 with |p x|=1/2+p/(2n) etc., followed by a check that the characteristic polynomial vanishes at 1/n. It also needs rows in the same group to give singular submatrices, and a check that such configurations exist (strict triangle inequality). The same unproved direction is used silently inside Case A, where the equality structure of C-hat is converted into 'three submatrices with smallest singular value equal to 1/sqrt(n-1)'. The converse is true (a direct computation gives P(1/n)=0 for cross-group pairs), but it is not argued.

issues.failure_explanation: Pairwise non-collinear a,b,c in R^2 satisfy a unique relation alpha a+beta b+gamma c=0, and a+b is parallel to a+c exactly when alpha=beta+gamma (similarly for the other pairs), so the claimed inference fails. Counterexample: squares a=(1,0), b=(0,1), c=a+2b=(1,2), realised by v_1=(1,0), v_2=(1/sqrt2,1/sqrt2) and v_3=sqrt(1+2i)~(1.272,0.786). Then a+b=(1,1) and a+c=(2,2) are positively parallel. Since the first right-singular vector of [v_i;v_j] has doubled-angle direction equal to the sum of squares, [v_1;v_2] and [v_1;v_3] have the same first (hence second) right-singular vector (angle pi/8). I verified this by computing V^T V for both pairs. So the lemma's conclusion fails. Even in the intended application, with positive dependence p x+q y+r z=0, the sums are collinear (antiparallel) whenever p=q+r. The paper also never verifies that the squares of the three chosen rows of C-hat are pairwise non-collinear; this needs the strict triangle inequality.
